scale.first_line: Scaling is a question of readiness, and I look at three things: proven practices, people, and position.
scale.script:
Scaling is a question of readiness, and I look at three things: proven practices, people, and position.

[slow] **Proven practices**: are we importing something that already works, so we're not starting from scratch? **People**: do we have the leaders to lead it? And **position**: is the organization truly ready to deliver on the promise of quality?

[beat] That also answers the autonomy question. **We open the school we know works, and then we build the school that's next on top of it.** There are places we can leapfrog, but that's the exception, not the rule. If we haven't built something that works, we shouldn't be scaling. And if we have, why wouldn't we start there? The principals have to agree that's the starting point, not just live with it.

So to a new principal I say: **earn it.** Get to stable, get to functional, then let's talk about innovation. You're going to be part of that evolution, and my side of the deal is investing in you.

[land] That's how Excel grew. The second and third schools started from 95% of the play, and today Excel's high school is in the **top 3% of public high schools in the country.** (If the room is warm: And even better, Jackie, who I had in sixth grade, now has my old job.) [STOP]
scale.landing: Excel's high school is in the top 3% nationally. (Warm room: Jackie now has my old job.)

adopt.first_line: Nobody had to say yes, so we had to earn it on the quality of our ideas.
adopt.script:
Nobody had to say yes, so we had to earn it on the quality of our ideas. The KIPP Foundation is the national arm: strategy, support and oversight, but no mandate authority. Twenty-eight independent regions, forty-eight high schools. So we did three things.

First, we **made the change theirs**. Every region was part of our listening tours and working groups, so when we announced the strategy, I was looking people in the eye, watching them nod. Second, we shrank the change. Stronger regions went first, got early wins, and those wins sold the rest. It built a positive flywheel. Third, we kept our finger on the pulse, the micro signals that tell you whether people are with you or turning off.

Take academic health. We wrote the manual, kept the training as simple as we could, and built a push-button tool that took the data from **present but obscured to right in front of them**. [slow] We piloted it, and we handed it off. Now the regions are running the play.

All 28 regions and all 48 high schools adopted the strategy. [beat] There was an alternate path, and no school chose it. [STOP]
adopt.landing: There was an alternate path, and no school chose it.

initiative.first_line: I took data that already existed and put it right in front of the people who needed it.
initiative.script:
I took data that already existed and put it right in front of the people who needed it. Every school in the network had grade books and tons of data, sitting in huge CSV and Excel files. It was there, but nobody could really use it.

So I used Claude Code to build a Python script that, with **the push of a button**, gave every teacher an individualized report: here are your students of concern, your assignments of concern, here's where your grades seem to be skewing. Weekly, high-quality data, compared to a standard. We did the same for students.

I designed it for one school and piloted it there, with a team and a regular meeting cadence. Then we handed it off, and it went across the country. Instead of waiting until the end of the quarter, teachers and students knew where they stood every week. The data went from **present but obscured to right in front of them**, [slow] and that drove a tremendous amount of positive change.

That year, 46% of ninth graders finished the quarter at a 3.0 or better. [beat] Up six points, the best quarter KIPP had ever had on that number. [STOP]
initiative.landing: Up six points, the best quarter KIPP had ever had on that number.

launch.first_line: I launch a school in three phases: stability, then the adults, then student ownership.
launch.script:
I launch a school in three phases: stability, then the adults, then student ownership. I came into Excel Academy with a mandate for change. Turnaround year, an entire new staff, a hundred students.

Stability first. Forty percent of the staff reported to me, so I took the routines, procedures and systems from my classroom and brought them to the whole school. I spent **six days writing the playbook** on how we'd do everything. My boss thought that was a crazy use of time. [beat] It became one of the most important things we did.

Then the adults. We worked on the five dysfunctions of a team and built a **best-idea-wins** culture, where it was **cool to be smart**. Then student ownership: honor council, student committees, orientation leaders. On the first day of school, we had kids telling kids how overwhelmed they were at first, that they'd even told their parents they didn't like the school.

We took that school from 270th in the state to number one, [slow] and got National Charter School of the Year. [STOP]
launch.landing: We took that school from 270th in the state to number one, and got National Charter School of the Year.
